source_text:
CAPUT SECUNDUM.
De S. Theologiae principiis, & quidem nominatim de complexo primo & ultimo.

I. Sunt autem in S. Theologia consideranda tum principia, e quibus illa arcessitur, tum partes in quas deducitur.

II. Principia S. Theologiae sunt propositiones a quibus sacra Christianae fidei dogmata per discursum sic deducuntur, deductaque in ea iterum resolvuntur, ut assensum hominis sani, modesti ac Deum timentis mereantur.

PRINCIPIUM in genere est id, a quo quicquam quoquo modo procedit; juxta Thomam 1. q. 33. art. 1. Est incomplexum aut complexum. Incomplexum est terminus simplex, idque vel principale, vel minus principale. Illud est ipse, vel, quod idem pollet, Christus, de quo 1. Cor. 1. Fulgentius lib. ad Thrasimundum pag. 108. Principium, ait, Christus, quia sempiternus praecedit: Finis Christus, quia perpetuus universa concludit. Principium Christus, quia ipse inchoavit: Finis Christus, quia perficit. Hoc est Verbum DEI, per quod Spiritus sanctus agit & operatur convertendo, illuminando, salvando homines, Rom. 1.16. 1. Cor. &c.

Utroque rite supposito, hic innuimus, primum principium complexum; quod est integra propositio, ex qua conclusio deducitur logice; unde & nonnullis principium logicum & cognitionis dicitur, quia ab hoc incipimus ea quae credimus logice deducere; ultra quod, ceu primum & generalissimum, in demonstratione non datur progressus. Hoc vero principium complectitur simul tum rationem quam qua est infallibile Dei testimonium, & rationem sub qua quae est revelationis lumen, eodemque sensu principium a quo & sub quo dicitur; ideoque longe aliter se habet, quam vel principium aliquod exterius, quod est occasionale nostrae fidei cognitionis & causa sine qua non, ut nobis hodie est auctoritas parentum, qui nobis veritatem salutiferam instillant, ut 2. Tim. 3.15. vel motorium, quod & ipsum topicum sive probabile argumentum est, ut miraculum.

Christiano his non opus est, quippe quae eliciunt assensum duntaxat humanae apprehensionis, fatente ipso Bellarmino. Quale igitur hoc nostrum est? Apodicticum & indemonstrabile, a seipso dignum fide, & cui nullo modo potest subesse falsum. Ad hoc principium adjungi debet causa sine qua non, nimirum auditio vel lectio, unde dicitur verbum auditus, 1. Thess. 2.13. Dogmata fidei exterius dico. Duo enim sunt dogmatum genera, alia ad credendum, alia ad sciendum. Illa sunt, quae speciali Dei revelatione nota sunt; haec quae ex rationis lumine patent. Illa creduntur, haec sciuntur. De illis hic proprie sermo est. Quae enim propositiones ad fidem proprie non pertinent, quales nonnullae in Bibliis occurrunt, eae huc non referuntur.
english: Chapter 2. On the principles of sacred theology, and specifically on the first and last complex principle.
I. Sacred theology asks us to weigh two things: the principles from which the discipline is drawn, and the parts into which it is divided.

II. By principles of sacred theology we mean those propositions that let us deduce the sacred dogmas of the Christian faith by ordered discourse — and then resolve the deduced dogmas back into the same propositions — so that a sound, modest, God-fearing person may rightly give assent.

Taken generally, a principle is whatever something proceeds from in any way (Thomas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 33, art. 1). Principles are either incomplex or complex. An incomplex principle is a simple term, either principal or less principal. The principal term is God himself — which is to say, Christ — of whom ([[1 Corinthians 1:30 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 1:30]]) speaks. Fulgentius writes to Thrasamund (p. 108): Christ is the beginning, for as everlasting he goes before; Christ is the end, for as perpetual he closes all things. Christ is the beginning, for he himself began; Christ is the end, for he perfects. The less principal term is the Word of God, the instrument through which the Holy Spirit converts, illuminates, and saves ([[Romans 1:16 >> Bible:Romans 1:16]]; compare 1 Corinthians and related places).

With those two incomplex principles in place, we turn to the first complex principle: a whole proposition from which a conclusion follows by logic. Some therefore call it a logical principle, or a principle of cognition, because our logical deduction of what we believe starts here, and demonstration cannot climb beyond this first and most general point. The complex principle holds together two respects at once — the respect from which, namely God's infallible testimony, and the respect under which, namely the light of revelation — and so is called a principle from which and under which. That sets it far apart from an exterior principle, which only occasions our knowledge of faith and is a necessary condition without which faith does not arise (today, for example, the parental authority that plants saving truth in us: [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]), and also far apart from a motive principle, which is only a topical or probable argument, such as a miracle.

A Christian does not depend on those lesser supports. They win only the assent of human apprehension — Bellarmine himself grants as much. What then is our principle? It is apodictic and indemonstrable, worthy of faith from itself, and such that falsehood cannot underlie it in any way. Still, a necessary condition must be joined to it — hearing or reading — which is why Scripture calls it the word of hearing ([[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]). I am speaking of the dogmas of faith as they reach us from outside. Dogmas come in two kinds: some for believing, others for knowing. The first kind is known by God's special revelation; the second lies open under the light of reason. The first is believed; the second is known. Our subject here is properly the former. Propositions that do not properly belong to faith — and some such do appear in the Bible — fall outside this account.

source_text:
III. Est eorum aliud primum & ultimum; aliud a primo dependens & ad illud subordinatum.

Haec principii theologici distinctio locum venit sub conditione Smyrnensi, Pergamenensi, Thyatirenensi & Sardensi potissimum, sub qua hodie vivimus. Nam Ephesina unicum principium, Verbum Dei scriptum, habuit, Act. 28.25. cujus indolem sub Pergamenensi statu laudavit beatus Augustinus: Utamur, inquiens, illa libertate ad quam nos vocavit Dominus, & eorum virorum, quorum laudes consequi non audemus, quorum multi literis scripturis non comparamus, quorum ingenium diligimus, quorum ore delectamur, quorum charitatem miramur, quorum martyria veneramur, hoc quod aliter sapuerunt, quam CANONICE non accipiamus: neque ullam eis facimus injuriam, cum eorum quaelibet dicta vel scripta a canonica divinarum Scripturarum auctoritate distinguimus.

IV. Primum & ultimum S. Theologiae principium est, ex quo posito reliqua omnia fidei dogmata deduci possint, ipsum vero non ab ullo alio directe deduci, ut authenticum & autopiston mereatur.

Primum & ultimum dicimus, quia ultra hoc in discursu Theologico inter Christianos non datur progressus; ne ducatur in infinitum aut in circulum redigatur, quod utrumque vitiosum est, id quod ita probamus. 1. Omne quod cognoscitur, sunt principia aut conclusiones, ut ex philosophia notum est. In dogmatis vero seu placitis Theologiae vitam divinam & aeternam spectantibus perinde etiam, ut in aliis disciplinis fieri consuevit, ex uno ad aliud progreditur, & unum ex alio argumentando probamus & concludimus. 2. Hae probationes & conclusiones, nisi aut in circulum commeare, aut in infinitum abire, quorum utrumque vitiosum, debeant, sistere alicubi oportet eas in aliquo primo, & quod ipsum aliunde non probetur & concludatur. 3. Primum vero hic potissimum intelligimus in ordine ad cognitionem hominis Christiani. 4. Neque enim hic postulamus, ut principia essendi & cognoscendi prorsus eadem sint; neque Theologiae indoles id ubique permittit. Deus enim auctor est & principium essendi creationis omnium. At quaestio hic est, unde nobis constet, Deum omnia creavisse. 5. Et quaestio non tam est, unde hoc illi vel huic probari possit, quam potissimum unde id Christiano constet, & in quemnam Christianus, utpote qui nec in circulo circumagitur, neque ut delirus in infinitum procedit, tandem, qua Christianus est & dicitur, fundetur. 6. Cum vero de principio in ordine ad nostram cognitionem, & quidem tali, unde alia per discursum deduci possint, hic agamus, palam fit quaeri de principio complexo, quod Aph. 2. axioma sive examinatam & propositam authenticam & autopiston nuncupavimus.
english: III. Among these principles one stands first and last; another hangs from that first principle and is ranked beneath it.

The distinction matters most under the Smyrnaean, Pergamene, Thyatiran, and above all the Sardian church-condition in which we now live. The Ephesian condition still had one principle alone — the written Word of God ([[Acts 28:25 >> Bible:Acts 28:25]]). Augustine praised that same character under the Pergamene state: Let us use the liberty to which the Lord has called us. As for those men whose praise we dare not equal, whose writings we refuse to set beside many Scriptures, whose genius we love, whose speech delights us, whose charity we admire, and whose martyrdoms we revere — whatever they thought otherwise, we must not receive it as canonical. We do them no injury when we mark off any saying or writing of theirs from the canonical authority of the divine Scriptures.

IV. Sacred theology's first and last principle is the one that, once granted, lets every other dogma of faith be deduced, while it itself is not deduced directly from any other — and therefore deserves to be called authentic and autopiston, self-attesting.

We name it first and last because Christian theological discourse cannot go beyond it without sliding into an infinite regress or a circle, and both paths are vicious. The proof runs in six steps. (1) Whatever is known is either a principle or a conclusion; philosophy already teaches that. In theology's dogmas concerning divine and eternal life, just as in other disciplines, we move from one point to another and prove one claim by arguing from another. (2) Those proofs and conclusions must halt in something first that is not itself proved from elsewhere — otherwise they circle or stretch to infinity, both of them faults. (3) First here means first for the Christian person's knowledge. (4) We are not requiring the principles of being and the principles of knowing to be identical everywhere; theology's own character often refuses that identity. God is author and principle of being for the whole creation. Yet our question is how it becomes established for us that God created all things. (5) Still more: the question is less how the point might be proved to this or that hearer, and more how it stands firm for the Christian — and on what he, who neither spins in a circle nor rushes on like a madman into infinity, is finally founded insofar as he is and is called a Christian. (6) Because we are asking for a principle ordered to our cognition, and for one from which further claims can be deduced by discourse, what we seek is plainly the complex principle that Aphorism 2 already named an axiom: an examined, proposed, authentic, autopiston principle.
